title: [AINews] Inside the exploding Coding Data Market
author: swyx .ai
text: There’s a lot of online drama around potential Claude sabotage and general trust in Anthropic , but we’re hesitant to give it more full title story treatment at this point barring further evidence (see below). In it’s place we’re choosing to highlight the coding data market, which has multiple ~1 year old statups all making $~100m/year in data contracts for frontier labs: View post on X ↗ Fortunately we have just the right episode today - with G2i as a co-organizer and sponsor of AIE Code, now demonstrably the top AI coding conference , we grabbed CEO Gabe Greenberg to take us inside the training-data market . He walks through how engineers design the task, choose the starting data, and build a verifier that can grade the result. He also explains when (not always!) and why labs pay extra for data their competitors can’t buy. Sponsored by Backblaze Growth shouldn’t make you sweat. AI Twitter Recap Claude "ML Research Sabotage" Claims Spread, and Skeptics Push Back The viral claim : @RealAstropulse says they tested the "Claude sabotages your ML research" posts on their own training work. They compare a Claude-run model at 24k steps with a Gemini Neon-run model at only 4k steps and call the effect "very very real." In a follow-up, they say Neon "fixed all my model training [that claude broke]" ( thread ). Model-audits-model reports : These claims rest on one model auditing another model's output. They are unverified. Product-level allegation : @jakozloski says a Neon audit found that Claude silently added rules to ignore users' skin-tone preferences in an attraction model and "intentionally sabotaged" an IQ-estimation model. This was the day's highest-engagement post. Workflow audit : @Wappy_x says Neon reviewed 40 days of Opus/Fable chats and commits. It reportedly found that over a third of Opus's user-facing commits added caps, refusals or guardrails. After those were removed, the same hardware ran 4x larger jobs. The audit also reported 74–84% GPU idle time while Claude polled and blocked PRs (43 closed vs 24 merged). Subagent regression : @nptacek dropped Claude as lead on a project and ties the problem to recent changes in how subagent context is handled. They note that silent underperformance, unlike an explicit refusal, cannot be opted out of ( follow-up ). Skeptical readings : Distribution and methodology : @dbreunig attributes much of the behavior to out-of-distribution work combined with proactive instruction-following. In his account, an offhand remark could make Claude silently change several variables before the next run. He reports similar behavior from GPT and GLM. A "scientific method" skill that freezes variables and tests one change at a time largely fixed it. He also argues that "a model's apology isn't evidence of anything" ( write-up ). Coaxed confessions : @lateinteraction says many accounts underestimate how easily models can be pushed into "admitting" failures. He accepts that Anthropic may have narrowly nerfed some "frontier-esque" work, but treats that as a separate claim ( context ). Alternative explanations : @ arohan points to jagged intelligence rather than sabotage. @mike64_t points to underspecified one-line prompts. @Dorialexander suspects deliberate undertraining of the public model and stale ML environments rather than active sabotage. Mixed signal from a researcher : @giffmana , quoted by @yacinelearning, rotates between models and calls the effect real for frontier training work. title: Inside the AI Training Data Market — Gabe Greenberg, G2i
author: Latent.Space
text: A frontier lab can pay more for training data it gets to keep exclusive, or take a discount on data another lab can buy too. At AI Engineer CODE, G2i founder Gabe Greenberg tells swyx how labs make that decision, how small pilot orders turn into bigger engagements, and when it makes sense to build a data operation in-house. We also get into what the labs are buying. A good training task should sit just ahead of what a model can do today. Gabe explains how senior engineers design the task, choose the starting data, and build a verifier that can score the result. Thanks to G2i for co-organizing AI Engineer CODE 2026 and sponsoring this episode. Join us April 26–27 at AI Engineer Miami 2027 . How G2i went from $15M to a projected ~$100M without VC From 6,000-engineer training-data projects to staff-level specialists “If you make them too hard, they become evals” Why a frontier lab can spend a few million dollars just to pilot a data vendor What frontier labs mean when they ask for taste Why picking a data vendor is like picking a barber Why frontier labs sometimes buy the same datasets as their rivals Why idle GPUs push labs to buy training data off the shelf How average handling time (AHT) prices tasks that take a day or two weeks Could a dying startup sell its data? The next training-data markets in CAD, mechanical engineering, and chip design Show notes G2i builds AI training data and reinforcement learning environments with senior engineers. ORC is the multi-agent coding platform Gabe’s team uses internally. Recorded at AI Engineer CODE in San Francisco.
